articles.title: ‘A new competition space’: US Coast Guard takes icebreaker on maiden voyage to the Arctic
articles.snippet: Having a more capable icebreaking ship represents a mission paradigm shift for the U.S. Coast Guard, said the captain of the new cutter.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Coast Guard’s first new icebreaker in nearly three decades returned from a maiden voyage to the Arctic this month, having demonstrated a spectrum of military operations that open up future possibilities for the service in the increasingly dynamic region.
The U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Storis, commissioned in August 2025, spent 133 days underway around the Arctic Ocean and Alaska, performing some missions — including law enforcement and live-fire gunnery — that haven’t been executed in the region in decades. In an interview with Military Times on Monday, the captain of the Storis, Capt. Corey Kerns, said experiments while underway, along with the built-in capabilities of the ship, create new options for Coast Guard operations in the Arctic.
Kerns, who took command of the ship before its commissioning, said staff from the Coast Guard Research and Development Center and the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit were onboard during the deployment to test aerial drones, including models made by Textron and Skyfront. The experimental flights were intended to assess how well the platforms withstood the harsh cold of the high Arctic, he said, but they also demonstrated practical uses for drones in the challenging task of ice navigation.
For icebreaking, “a good aerial drone could be helpful,” Kerns said. “Piloting is something we still do from our bridges, but we’re seeing that technology used in ways to make it much more efficient to pass through the ice.”
The unmanned aerial vehicles helped the ship to maintain its intended station because “they can see out better and farther,” he said.
“It was pretty interesting for the crew to see it, learn how we would be able to use and interact with a more capable drone. We did deploy with some of our own drones … less capable versions, and they didn’t do as well in the Arctic. So it was good to see that we’re working on a solution that is more robust given the environmental concerns.”
But the Storis, a retrofitted commercial icebreaking ship formerly known as Aiviq, contains other “new capabilities we didn’t expect,” Kerns said, citing the ship’s container storage spaces that open possibilities for different deployable payloads or expeditionary gear sets. He also noted the multiple cranes built into the Storis add logistics and maneuvering capabilities.
“Now we’ll work with the partners to be like, ‘What’s on your dream sheet? What would you love for us to be able to do up there?’” he said. “And I think we’ll be able to execute some of that. I think that was the biggest lesson learned: There’s more to it; we left a little bit on the plate, as it were.”
Mock refueling shows potential
One potentially game-changing additional mission could be a refueling capability that could service U.S. Navy vessels in the Arctic, Kerns said.
“The ship was designed to support an oil rig in the Arctic, so she has a lot of what we would call expeditionary logistics capability,” he said. “We did some of that on this patrol, too, where I did a mock refuel of one of our national security cutters, and we’ve demonstrated that we could do that for the Navy if they needed a destroyer up there.”
The ability to refuel a destroyer, made possible by the Storis’s large storage capacity and its native capability to pump the fuel up and into an oil rig, could potentially save the Navy up to a week-and-a-half of transit and time off-station to get to a shore-based refueling point, he said.
“Once you’re in the Arctic, it is a long ways back to the closest location where you can refuel a vessel,” Kerns said.
He stressed that refueling was likely not a mission the Storis could undertake on a regular basis, but suggested it could be a valuable fallback amid operational necessity.
“If one of those vessels was up here and there was something else that was up here that required them to stay – it would be better for our national security if that capable vessel could stay in the area rather than travel a week-and-a-half to refuel. Storis can give them the gas and keep them on station so they can stay on mission,” he said.
Law enforcement missions
Storis’s five-month deployment also included the first law enforcement mission by a polar icebreaker in more than two decades, according to Coast Guard officials, who said the ship executed multiple fishing vessel inspections in the Bering Sea. The crew also teamed up with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Office of Law Enforcement for a joint boarding and fisheries plant inspection.
Kerns said standing up a law enforcement mission required special training and the addition of a maritime law enforcement specialist – a chief petty officer first class – to prepare the crew.
“Luckily, we had a chief, an E-7, on board who had a lot of boarding experience,” Kerns said. “We had to see how we would do it on board stores, which is not designed to be a law enforcement ship, but has some capable boats … Whenever we had the opportunity, some open water, we might run a law enforcement drill, preparing for later in the deployment when we knew we’d be focused on that. And it kind of all came together.”
Challenges inherent to fixing the small boats when they broke due to age and disuse were among the hurdles the crew of the Storis had to overcome during the deployment. Others, Kerns said, included working around the layout of a ship not inherently designed for military use, which could get in the way of well-established Coast Guard and firefighting protocol.
Command and control
A potentially more serious issue was the lack of built-in military command-and-control communications equipment, which he said presented itself as an issue during a shorter underway the Storis had embarked on last summer.
The ship, he said, had been operating near some Chinese research vessels, and leaders realized they didn’t have a direct and secure way to communicate in case of crisis or escalation.
“When you’re operating that close, and geopolitics are tied in, you don’t want to make a mistake,” Kerns said. “But I also didn’t have the ability to communicate directly with my superior officers back in Juneau or Alameda (California).”
When the Storis departed on its full deployment, he said, it was with improved military communications. But, he added, additional work needed to be done to enhance its command-and-control suite.
During the Arctic deployment, the Storis spent some 300 hours monitoring the four Chinese research vessels in the region, which did not register their planned activity with the United States, as other nations around Alaska’s Exclusive Economic Zone do.
“That’s going to be a growing mission set. I think you’re starting to see more and more, and I would expect at some point that you’ll see maybe even more military move up into that beyond just Coast Guard,” Kerns said. “So it’s a new competition space for us, and we’re just at the start of it.”
The proven ability of the Storis to complete an Arctic deployment frees up the Coast Guard’s aging medium icebreaker Healy to focus on scientific research missions, Kerns said, and removes the burden of military presence and monitoring operations.
The Healy had been set to deploy to the Arctic this fall, but it suffered a mechanical problem and had to be towed back to its homeport in Seattle. The mishap came two years after the Healy was forced to cancel a 2024 deployment due to an electrical fire onboard.
For the Coast Guard, which is set to get the first of three purpose-built icebreakers around 2033, having a more capable icebreaking ship represents a mission paradigm shift for the service, Kerns said.
“It’s important for icebreaker sailors who aren’t used to that to explain that, ‘Hey, in the future, the future of icebreaking isn’t icebreaking in and of itself,” he said. “You’re a multi-mission ship … We owe that to our civilian leadership. We have all these capabilities. We should be able to execute those capabilities anywhere in the world that they desire.”

articles.title: From horsepower to firepower, Japan draws auto suppliers into major arms buildup
articles.snippet: "Drones are a much better business,” chief executive Takenobu Hongo said of Aster’s embrace of defense contracting, which has long been viewed warily by citizens of a country shaped by decades of pacifism.
articles.full_text:
YOKOTE, Japan — For years, Japanese manufacturer Aster made its money supplying parts for Toyota vehicles.
But as the country’s auto industry struggles in the face of fierce Chinese competition, Aster has found a new niche in defense technology. Its electric motors power drones built by U.S. military technology company Anduril, and defense work has grown to a tenth of revenue since it entered the sector last year.
“Drones are a much better business,” chief executive Takenobu Hongo said of Aster’s embrace of defense contracting, which has long been viewed warily by citizens of a country shaped by decades of pacifism. “At the moment, for us, automotive motors aren’t very profitable.”
Aster’s pivot is part of a move by Tokyo to encourage Japan’s many auto suppliers to join the country’s biggest military buildup since World War II, according to interviews with nine people, including government officials, company executives and an advisor to Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Cabinet.
Takaichi’s government hopes that tapping existing industrial supply chains will speed up Japan’s security transformation as it bolsters its defenses against threats from nuclear-armed neighbors China, Russia and North Korea. The rearmament efforts are backed by Tokyo’s chief security partner, the United States, which is pressing allies to increase spending on armed forces.
The buildup also offers an important diversification avenue to Japan’s once world-leading auto industry. The country’s factories built nearly 900,000 fewer vehicles in 2025 than a decade earlier, according to the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association.
Reuters is reporting for the first time details of the industry’s nascent push into the defense sector and how it is supported by the Acquisition, Technology & Logistics Agency (ATLA), which oversees defense ministry procurement. The department has been evaluating suppliers like Aster, pairing them with arms firms and offering new funding streams, an agency official and four executives said.
An advisor to Takaichi’s Cabinet, Koko Kato, has also played a role in helping steer the industry’s transformation. If there is a synergy between defense and autos, carmakers “should take the opportunity,” she said. Kato told Reuters she oversaw changes in February to a separate trade ministry program aimed at helping auto suppliers diversify into defense and other industries.
ATLA said in response to Reuters questions that it serves as a point of contact to help companies seeking to enter the defense industry and that it will continue to work with other government departments to encourage new entrants.
Takaichi’s office did not respond to questions.
Manufacturing powerhouse
Takaichi’s government has pledged to lay out a new security strategy by year-end, including a road map for bolstering an arms industry that was initially dismantled after Japan’s World War II defeat.
The plan builds on Japan’s legacy as a manufacturing powerhouse. Despite its auto industry’s recent decline, Japan is still the world’s third-largest vehicle-producing nation. The industry manufactures more than 8 million vehicles a year and supports one in 10 jobs, with some 70,000 companies making an enormous array of components.
Skills prized in auto manufacturing, such as precision and electronics manufacturing, as well as quality control, are relevant to arms production, said Pontus Haggstrom, a Japan-based adviser to the auto industry and former CEO of Stellantis Japan.
The industry “also knows how to produce complex products reliably and at scale,” he added.
The case for Japan to draw on domestic manufacturing has also grown as American arms makers struggle to replenish arsenals depleted by conflicts in the Middle East and Europe. Tokyo was the destination for about a tenth of U.S. weapon exports in 2021-25, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
“Customers tell us their traditional suppliers don’t have the capacity,” said Hiroko Suzuki, the chief executive of car-engine component maker Kyowa Industrial, which has received a growing number of orders for prototype drone engines.
While Kyowa has long made missile-related components, the defense sideline now comprises 10% of annual sales, up from 3% in spring 2025.
Some auto suppliers are also eyeing opportunities to sell to U.S. and European military contractors.
ATLA has been holding events in Tokyo to connect Japanese suppliers with potential Western clients. Some 48 Japanese companies from various industries took part in a September event, twice as many as last year, the procurement agency said.
Drone rush
ATLA, which in October launched a funding program for the development and testing of new military technology, has encouraged some auto suppliers to produce components for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The agency has said it is willing to provide millions of dollars in support to projects that advance to prototype development.
The upcoming national security strategy is expected to outline plans to arm Japan with fleets of attack and interceptor drones of the kind that have reshaped warfare elsewhere.
But domestic industrial production is tiny: The country exported just over 1,100 drones last year, compared with the roughly 123,000 UAVs sold to overseas clients by neighboring Taiwan, according to trade figures compiled by Taiwan’s Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology.
While fiscal constraints are likely to force Tokyo to rethink some existing orders for missiles and aircraft, such is Japan’s need for UAVs that drone-related spending will likely be ringfenced, according to an official familiar with budget plans.
Toru Tokushige, CEO of Japanese dronemaker Terra Drone, said ATLA officials recently introduced him to Kaaz, a maker of racing car parts that has developed a small gasoline-powered aircraft engine. Tapping auto suppliers could significantly increase Japan’s drone-building capacity, he said.
A spokesperson for Kaaz said that it has consulted with ATLA and is actively pursuing the development of engines for military drones.
Ishikawa Energy Research, a drone startup that attended ATLA’s September forum, is also seeking military applications for its aircraft.
The firm’s UAVs are used mainly for agricultural purposes such as crop spraying, founder Mitsuru Ishikawa told Reuters. But the former Honda engineer said his gasoline-powered drones could also transport heavier defense equipment or conduct longer-range military reconnaissance missions than more common battery-powered models.
The firm, which is based in the industrial town of Ota, has already tapped into the sprawling local auto supply chain that feeds carmaker Subaru, with more than 50% of the components in its drones coming from auto suppliers.
Ishikawa does not think those firms will object to his military ambitions, in part because Subaru, which is better known globally for its sporty cars, already has a major defense arm. The company has built military aircraft, including attack helicopters, for Japan’s Self-Defense Forces for decades.
Subaru expects defense-related demand to grow and intends to capture those business opportunities, a spokesperson said, declining to give specific forecasts.
Overcoming a taboo
The auto industry’s shift to defense contracting is for now largely limited to smaller parts makers, according to five officials and analysts.
Japan’s big three automakers — Toyota, Honda and Nissan — have shown little appetite for a defense tilt. They still have substantive businesses in China, which has criticized Japan’s arms buildup. They have also long been wary of the reputational risks that come with the defense sector.
“The company’s basic position at this point is that we will not do anything related to defense,” senior Toyota executive Hiroyuki Ueda said at a results briefing earlier this month.
Nissan declined to comment on potential defense work, while Honda said in response to questions that it has no specific plans to enter the sector.
That hesitancy also filters down to their closest suppliers.
Mitsubishi Electric chief financial officer Kenichiro Fujimoto told Reuters his company was pursuing a new military drone venture and that tapping auto supply chains made sense. However, he added, automakers were quite resistant to their suppliers doing anything outside the industry.
“There’s this odd attitude sometimes, like, ‘Don’t do any work other than ours,’” he said.
Aster’s Hongo was also wary that some of his company’s roughly 100 staff might object when he gathered them at his factory in the northern Japanese town of Yokote in November 2025 to announce that Anduril wanted to use their motors.
Instead, the 71-year-old executive received a warm reception. “Everyone was more like: ‘Wow, that’s impressive!’” he said of the meeting.
The commercial opportunities in defense, as well as growing public concern about Japan’s security challenges, would lure many more companies, Hongo predicted.
“In Japan now, there are very few people who think this is somebody else’s problem,” he said.
Reporting by Tim Kelly, John Geddie, Daniel Leussink and Maki Shiraki

articles.title: Russia may launch nuke-laden satellite by year’s end, German report warns
articles.snippet: Russia may place a satellite loaded with a nuclear weapon into orbit by the end of the year, German public media reported, citing intelligence sources.
articles.full_text:
GLASGOW, Scotland — Russia may place a satellite loaded with a nuclear weapon into orbit by the end of the year, German public media reported, citing intelligence sources.
The satellite, dubbed Sputnik-S, has reportedly been assembled and stored in the greater Moscow area for several years. An investigation by German public broadcasters WDR and NDR and German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung uncovered an intelligence assessment from early November that says the satellite could be launched “within 60 days.”
Asked about the reporting during a visit to Berlin, NATO chief Mark Rutte said on Monday that the alliance was constantly assessing its deterrence and defence situation.
“I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory. And that includes making sure that we are safe when it comes to the space element,” Rutte told reporters at a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit is prohibited by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, to which Russia and 117 other countries are parties.
Detonating an atomic bomb in space can have devastating effects: It is likely to destroy or incapacitate a large number of satellites, as well as cripple communications systems and power grids back on Earth with its electromagnetic pulse.
Both the United States and the Soviet Union detonated nuclear weapons in space during the Cold War, most significantly the American Starfish Prime test, 400 kilometers over the Pacific Ocean in 1962. The resulting artificial radiation belt damaged several satellites, including the Telstar-1 satellite launched a day after the blast.
Reporting by Western intelligence agencies of alleged Russian plans to place a nuke into orbit dates back several years. In early 2024, then-House Intelligence Committee chairman Mike Turner (R-Ohio) publicly warned of a “serious national security threat” without identifying it; U.S. media soon reported this was referring to a Russian space nuke. The U.S. intelligence community reportedly started circulating corresponding warnings a year earlier, in February 2023, German public media reports.
Shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a mysterious satellite called simply Kosmos-2553 was launched, which Western governments had flagged as a potential space threat. Kosmos is the generic identifier for unnamed Russian satellites, including military ones with undisclosed functions.
The Russian authorities said Kosmos-2553 was for scientific research into radiation. However, Western intelligence agencies were “greatly skeptical” of this civilian explanation, according to the new reporting by German media.
Security services told WDR and NDR that they believe the satellite was being used to test the effects of nuclear weapons use in space. According to them, the satellite “functions as a so-called dummy, intended to test how radiation affects satellites – and at what point a satellite sustains severe damage.” The aim of the tests was to determine the extent to which the satellite remains operational and maneuverable under intense radiation.
The Russian Embassy in Berlin said it had no information on the topic, and said it rejected all accusations regarding the space activities of the Russian Federation, calling them part of a “propaganda campaign,” reporters from WDR, NDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung wrote. Russian measures for the exploration and utilization of space are conducted in accordance with international commitments and “exclusively for peaceful purposes,” the Embassy said.
With reporting by Reuters

articles.title: China’s fourth aircraft carrier, bigger than others and nuclear-powered, nears completion
articles.snippet: China’s fourth aircraft carrier, a gigantic vessel known so far as just Type 004, will come out as early as next year bigger than its predecessors and with nuclear power that can launch planes faster than usual in case of any conflict, analysts say.
articles.full_text:
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — China’s fourth aircraft carrier, a gigantic vessel known so far as just Type 004, will come out as early as next year bigger than its predecessors and with nuclear power that can launch planes faster than usual in case of any conflict, analysts say.
And it’s tipped to add pressure on countries, such as Japan and the United States, that already keep a high alert for the Chinese military.
The carrier being built now in the northern port city Dalian could accommodate 75 to 90 planes once deployed, the Asia program director at the think tank Defence Priorities has said.
As of October, the vessel’s hull measured about 322 meters in length from the unfinished bow to stern with a width of approximately 46 meters, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), also a think tank.
CSIS called Type 004 “far larger than any other class of surface combatant” in China’s navy.
Aerial photos of the carrier show the “basic hull form” already built, auguring well for a 2027 launch, said Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Deployment would take five to 10 years, he said.
The specs would make Type 004 “slightly larger” than China’s Fujian aircraft carrier, currently the biggest one in its fleet, Koh said.
Information available today about the Type 004 – likely to be renamed after a Chinese province like the existing three – classify the vessel as a “supercarrier” in terms of electronics, tonnage and aircraft carrying capacity, said Alexander Huang, chairman of the Council of Strategic and Wargaming Studies in Taipei.
Nuclear power on board would offer the aircraft more propulsion than China’s existing electromagnetic aircraft launch system, Koh said. He said that would eliminate the need for power generators on board the carrier while allowing faster takeoffs – without payload compromises – and quick combat turnarounds for refueling.
“It seems to signal a certain strategic objective,” Koh said of the nuclear capability. “It’s not just going to move along your coast. It seems to signal a certain global ambition.”
Nuclear power will give the carrier “essentially unlimited endurance” and allow for global deployment without the kind of tanker support a conventionally powered carrier needs, said David Silbey, a Cornell University professor specializing in military history and defense policy.
The fourth carrier may get posted to northern China because the other three are in the south, Huang said. In that scenario, he said, China could “use one of the four to always operate somewhere.”
Type 004 may be used for training and maintenance as well as operations, Huang added.
China’s fourth carrier gets it closer to rivaling the U.S. navy, analysts said.
It will compare in size to the Nimitz and Ford class U.S. carriers, which means it can carry as many as 100 aircraft, Silbey said. “That gives it much more striking power than previous carriers, which could only carry around 50,” he said.
The U.S. navy has 11 carriers, all nuclear powered.
Even if smaller than the U.S. fleet, a Chinese navy with nuclear-powered carriers can mount a challenge to the United States, Koh said.
The U.S. navy maintains bases in Guam, Hawaii and Japan plus treaty alliances with Japan and the Philippines. The U.S. and China have long seen each other as rival superpowers.
Experts have said China sent an especially large number of its naval deployments near Japan’s southernmost islands and nearby waters since a political rift that erupted in November 2025 over a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
The Philippines is embroiled in a maritime sovereignty dispute with China.
China plans to build more carriers over the next decade for a “blue water capability that they’ve never really had before,” Silbey said. “In the Pacific, it means that they can go after American assets that are out of range of their other assets.”

articles.title: The Army has told us how it fights. We can’t do that in an analog tank.
articles.snippet: Decades of upgrades have pushed the Abrams tank to its limits. A generational redesign is the only way forward, a former three-star general argues.
articles.full_text:
Last month, the Army published “How the Army Fights.” It describes a force that wins through four things: convergence, strike, close battle and endurance, all inside a multi-domain (MDO) fight against an enemy with advanced reconnaissance, drones and precision munitions. Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the vice chief of staff (and now, chief of staff nominee) who provided the guidance, was blunt that the geometry of the battlespace has changed, but ground maneuver is not dead.
Now look at what we would send into that fight. Every combat vehicle in the Armored Brigade Combat Team is an analog machine with digital parts bolted on after the fact. None of them can fight effectively in a MDO environment, and sustainment dollars can’t fix that.
A symbol of these issues is the 45-year-old Abrams. It has run out of room for incremental upgrades, which is why the Army cancelled the M1A2 SEPv4 in 2023 and accelerated the M1E3. For decades those upgrades served the Joint Force well: digital architectures, advanced thermal sights, reactive armor and auxiliary systems layered onto a 1970s chassis. That approach is now slipping under its own weight.
The M1E3 is the tank the Army’s own warfighting guidance requires. We should evaluate it against the Army’s four elements.
Close Battle: The Tank Has To Survive To Get There
The guidance calls close battle the point where enemy forces are physically defeated and terrain is seized. Alongside our infantry, close battle is the tank’s job. It has been since WWI, WWII and both Iraq wars — and it will be again.
But a tank that can’t reach the fight, or can’t survive it, isn’t doing its intended job. Ukraine has dismantled our assumptions about passive armor. Cheap first-person view drones, fiber-optic loitering munitions and top-attack anti-tank guided missiles have inverted the survivability equation. Cage armor and bolt-on active protection systems are stopgaps, but they add parasitic weight, raise the silhouette, draw heavy electrical power and create blind spots. And in an M1A2, three of the four crew still sit in the turret under thin roof armor, right where the threat can be lethal.
How the Pentagon is advancing layered counter-UAS defenses through AI, directed energy and advanced sensing
There is no single answer to the drone threat, pushing the Pentagon toward a broader mix of defenses.
The M1E3 answers with design, not add-ons. An unmanned turret with an ammunition handling system moves the three-person crew down into the better-protected hull. Turret ballistic requirements drop, and so does weight. An integrated hard-kill active protection system covers 360 degrees plus high-angle top-attack threats, replacing the applique systems we bolt on today and the weight they carry.
Strike: Tempo Requires Mobility, And We’re Overweight
The guidance says effective strike depends on tempo and continuous mobility: the ability to disperse rapidly, aggregate to deliver effects and keep moving. Existing Abrams models simply don’t fit the guidance.
With the Trophy Active Protection System, the fielded M1A2 SEPv3 weighs over 76 tons. That’s more than most European and Indo-Pacific bridges can support, and more than organic recovery assets can tow. It also sits at the absolute engineering margin of tactical bridging and Heavy Equipment Transporters. The result is that commanders can often only commit armored brigade combat teams along the few avenues of approach that can bear the load. That funnels armor into predictable chokepoints, exactly where an adversary’s precision fires are already registered. Getting from port to a forward assembly area takes longer, and in a fight measured in days, every delay costs initiative.
Decades of counter-IED underbelly plating, composite armor packages and bolt-on survivability systems created this problem, and marginal modifications can’t undo it. The M1E3 targets a combat weight of roughly 60 tons. A 14-to-16-ton reduction requires a clean-sheet architecture, but it can restore the strategic, operational and tactical mobility that large-scale combat demands.
Convergence: A Tank Has To Be A Node, Not An Island
Convergence connects sensors to decision-makers and layers lethal and nonlethal effects at tempo. That is how MDO works: sense, fuse, decide and act faster than the enemy can react. It only works if platforms in the formation can plug into the network and leverage the capacity that transcends domains, agencies and echelons.
The SEPv3 added updated data buses and Line Replaceable Units, but it is still an analog-era chassis dressed up with digital parts. Every new capability means depot overhauls, custom power converters and tangled wiring harnesses, and the Army can’t wait years for an upgrade when the threat changes in months.
The M1E3 adopts Modular Open Systems Architecture from the start. Upgrades become software-defined and arrive in weeks, not depot cycles. Integrated battle management and automated targeting aids let a three-person crew take in and act on feeds from unmanned aerial systems and robotic ground vehicles without being overwhelmed. This makes the tank a node in the kill web, sharing what it sees and shooting what the network finds.
In the end, if we want to compel our will upon an intransigent opponent, we have to be where they are. The M1E3 becomes a protected node, penetrating enemy defenses, which brings to bear all domains under protection with improved mobility and firepower.
Endurance: The Tank That Doesn’t Need A Fuel Convoy
The guidance defines endurance as the ability to absorb the enemy’s best hit and keep fighting. The M1A2’s AGT1500 turbine delivers remarkable acceleration and torque, but it consumes fuel even while at idle. Its consumption exceeds the brigade’s organic fuel capacity, which ties every ABCT to large divisional fuel convoys. Those convoys are slow, predictable and visible. Against persistent aerial sensors and loitering munitions, a fuel tanker is a target whose vulnerability is unacceptable.
The M1E3’s hybrid diesel-electric powertrain cuts fuel consumption by 50 percent and shrinks the sustainment tail with it. High-capacity batteries can run sensors, communications and counter-UAS suites for extended periods with the engine off. For short distances, the tank can move on battery power with near-zero acoustic and thermal signature. And where the SEPv3 already runs near peak electrical load, the M1E3’s high-voltage architecture has the surplus power for what comes next. (Disclosure: I’m a board member on Sapa Transmission, which is one of many suppliers that would benefit from the M1E3 program; I have been advocating for this program long before that business interest.)
The Cost Of Standing Still
Critics will say that with limited money available, air defense, long-range fires and munitions stockpiles need to come first. Those are real priorities, but deferring the tank to fund them is a false alternative.
Sustaining the M1A2 means a growing stack of custom engineering patches, depot overhauls and rising sustainment costs. Those costs will soon exceed the amortized development and procurement cost of the M1E3. The Army would be paying more every year to keep a platform that can’t execute what its own guidance requires. The sunk-cost fallacy should not set requirements for the next war.
Fielding the M1E3 also secures the industrial base. The Joint Systems Manufacturing Center in Lima, Ohio, and its national supply chain need a predictable workload. Turning that footprint from a 20th-century overhaul-and-upgrade depot into an advanced manufacturing hub preserves a capability that would take years to rebuild if it were lost.
The Abrams anchored American ground dominance for half a century. But its weight, its fuel appetite and its vulnerability to today’s threats call for a generational leap, not another upgrade.
The idea that future land wars can be won with stand-off fires or cheap consumable mass is a dangerous illusion. In the vice chief’s words, close battle “is not a relic of an earlier age.” Someone still must seize and hold ground against an enemy who is trying to kill them, and that takes a main battle tank working inside a combined-arms formation and backed by the Joint Force.
The Army has described how it fights. Congress and Pentagon leadership now need to give it a tank that can fight that way, and develop and field the M1E3.
Retired Army Lt. Gen. Eric J. Wesley served as deputy commanding general of Army Futures Command and led the rewrite of the Army’s warfighting concept referred to as Multi-Domain Operations. He also commanded the Maneuver Center of Excellence, home of the Infantry and Armor schools. He currently serves on a number of defense related boards, including the Sapa Transmission Board.

articles.title: White House seeks funding exemptions for Golden Dome, Trump battleship in next funding stopgap
articles.snippet: The Pentagon’s munitions ramp up could also face turmoil if anomalies for key programs are not approved, the White House warned.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Golden Dome and the Trump-class battleship are among the programs for which the White House wants to see additional money or other authorities if Congress passes another stopgap funding bill in December, according to a list sent to Capitol Hill on Monday.
The list, which was reported by Politico on Monday evening, lays out almost two dozen defense programs for which the White House is seeking anomalies — or funding exemptions — if another continuing resolution (CR) is passed. The document notes that additional Defense Department anomaly requests are forthcoming.
Because a CR keeps federal funding stable at of the previous fiscal year and prohibits money from going to new programs, an administration requests anomalies when it wants to funnel more money into a program to start or accelerate it. Lawmakers have until the current CR expires on Dec. 11 to either pass full year appropriations — an unlikely prospect, given ongoing disagreements between Republicans and Democrats on funding — or to pass another stopgap bill.
In the anomalies list, the White House requested $5 billion for Golden Dome, its hallmark missile defense effort. Because the program “has no new funding under the current CR,” the White House states that “[w]ithout this anomaly, Golden Dome will be unable to continue production.”
It also asked for advanced procurement authority for the Trump-class battleship, noting that “[w]ithout this anomaly material delays would impact cost and on-time delivery of the Battleship.”
The Pentagon’s goal of ramping up weapons production could also face major headwinds if anomalies are not approved.
While the administration did not request additional funding for critical munitions programs, it is seeking “spend faster” authorities for several weapons — including PAC-3, Tomahawk, JASSM, LRASM, Precision Strike Missile and the Standard Missile family. The authorities would allow the Pentagon to obligate funding more quickly to meet planned increases in production rate.
How the Pentagon is advancing layered counter-UAS defenses through AI, directed energy and advanced sensing
There is no single answer to the drone threat, pushing the Pentagon toward a broader mix of defenses.
Without anomalies, those munitions could face delays in funding that “would require contract renegotiation, disrupt prime and subcontractor planning, and reduce economies of scale. Higher unit costs will reduce purchasing power,” the White House warned.
For instance, the government is at risk of incurring a $400 million multiyear contract cancellation penalty for both LRASM and JASSM if anomalies are not approved. The White House also identified potential termination liabilities of $554 million for the SM-3 IIA and almost $1.6 billion for the SM-3 IB, according to the White House document.
If a CR stretches into summer without anomalies for multiyear production for Tomahawk missiles, the Army and Navy will not be able to award funding by a June 2027 deadline and could face cancellation charges of up to $4.4 billion, the White House stated.
Additionally, the Pentagon is seeking new-start and additional multiyear procurement authorities for counter-drone systems, which would allow the department to increase counter-small unmanned aircraft systems (C-sUAS) procurement from about 363 effectors to in fiscal 2026 to 853 in fiscal 2027.
It also asks for an increase of about $22 billion for the Virginia-class submarine, Columbia-class submarine and Ford-class carrier programs to keep ship construction on schedule.
A separate $400 million funding request is associated with “CVN-81 redesign activities” that have been deemed “a Presidential priority” — a likely reference to Trump’s intent to replace the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) on the future carrier USS Doris Miller with steam catapults.
While Congress usually looks kindly on anomalies meant to keep efforts like shipbuilding programs going during a CR, the current bipartisan stopgap approved by lawmakers in September did not include anomalies sought by the White House for the Trump-class battleship and munitions production.

articles.title: LaNeve’s campaign plan aims for top-down guidance, flipping ‘transformation in contact’ era
articles.snippet: If the guidance does become the service’s official campaign plan, “How the Army Fights” will leave behind the service’s “Continuous Transformation” campaign, including initiatives such as Transformation in Contact, in an effort to give soldiers clearer direction in how they train and fight.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The decision by Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army’s top uniformed officer, to move away from the Army’s “Continuous Transformation” campaign plan in favor of more top-down guidance was driven in part by burnout from soldiers, one of LaNeve’s top advisors told Breaking Defense in a recent interview.
If the new campaign plan, released in an early form last month as a document titled “How the Army Fights,” is officially codified, it would flip the current campaign plan on its head, Col. Pete Walther, one of LaNeve’s special assistants, told Breaking Defense in a Nov. 17 interview.
Unlike the previous “bottom-up” concept, which lacked distinct objectives for each echelon, the new guidance emphasizes top-down direction to standardize and align the Army’s approach to fighting and training, something Walther said was designed to make sure the service is more aligned across the board.
“‘How the Army Fights’ is something our Army needs. It plants the flag for where we are going and unifies the team around a common understanding of our contribution to the Joint Force against the pacing challenge,” LaNeve said during the annual AUSA conference in October. “It defines the operational environment and articulates how operational-level maneuver bridges tactical and strategic success.”
The guidance is scheduled to become the Army’s official campaign plan by Feb. 1, replacing “Continuous Transformation,” developed under former Army Chief Gen. Randy George, who was ousted by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in April. Right now, “How the Army Fights” is in the “execute order” stage, Walther explained, the step before it becomes the official campaign plan.
Though “How the Army Fights” was born under LaNeve, his spokesperson told Breaking Defense that the intent is “that it’s not tied to an individual, it’s about large organizational change.” Therefore, even if LaNeve is not confirmed in the Senate, such changes that the new guidance is trying to implement ideally won’t become moot.
The transition marks a shift in how the Army approaches modernization and experimentation. Under the “Continuous Transformation” campaign, the service underwent the sprawling Army Transformation Initiative (ATI), which cut programs and top officers and rearranged money and priorities. The effort also included Transformation in Contact (TiC), an initiative that rapidly put new experimental commercial technology and gear into soldiers’ hands during rotations at Combat Training Centers (CTCs), allowing units to experiment with new capabilities in the field. (CTCs are large-scale, realistic combat training exercises).
But Walther said the emphasis on bottom-up experimentation under the previous campaign sometimes came at the expense of clear direction from Army leadership.
“[LaNeve] is absolutely focused on divisions, corps and theater armies. I think we focused a great deal on companies, battalions and brigades during the Army Transformation Initiative,” Walther said. “It was beneficial, and we don’t want to lose what we gained through that. But for him, he wants to build on that, and the next logical step is the divisions, the corps and the theater armies.”
As it is now, soldiers at each echelon don’t necessarily have clear cut responsibilities, Walther said, hindering the Army from carrying out its goal of “operational maneuver” — the service’s ability to avoid becoming static or attritional in warfare. LaNeve wants commanders of battalions and below, and sometimes brigades, to focus on close battle operations, where strike should happen at the brigade level and above and convergence should happen at the division levels and above. Endurance, Walther said, is needed at every echelon.
“We haven’t necessarily for a while had that level of focus,” Walther said. “What we’re doing is providing clarity. We had battalion commanders that thought they were hunting 300 kilometers deep [for strike missions]. We need them in close battle. We need corps to be manned, trained and equipped to be able to do convergence with the joint force.”
Although initiatives such as ATI and TiC will end, modernization will not, LaNeve’s spokesperson emphasized to Breaking Defense. ‘“Continuous Transformation’ was motion, but ‘How the Army Fights’ is direction,” they said.
But make no mistake, TiC and ATI are definitively ending, not simply going through a rebranding effort.
Instead of commanders at the brigade level and below deciding what kind of experimental tech they want to test out during CTCs, that guidance will now come from the division level or above, often coming directly from the Army’s headquarters. Commanders will then report back up to division headquarters and above on how such experimental tech is performing.
The End Of TiC
Walther acknowledged that TiC produced “good lessons learned” and made it possible for “a lot of material tactical lethality” to be pushed down quickly. However, its bottom-up experimentation approach also created what is sometimes known as tech fatigue — when soldiers become overburdened with having too much new tech, or “kit,” not enough time to experiment with it, paired with confusion on what missions the tech is built for.
“It was done on the side of angels. It was a good intention, but it was a disservice to that brigade commander and his team. You can’t evaluate their core competencies if you just gave them brand new kit. That was ostensibly what was happening as Gen. LaNeve was doing some of his initial battlefield circulation,” Walther said.
He added that over the past few years, TiC was “somewhat predicated on, ‘Just throw material to companies and battalions, let them iterate on it, and tell the Army what they think about it.’”
Walther denied that LaNeve’s decision to move away from TiC was politically motivated by previous tensions between Hegseth and George and former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, both champions of the effort. Instead, he argued that the experimentation model was always intended to be transitional.
“Eventually, you have to stop transforming at the lowest echelons, and you’ve got to get back to a more deliberate modernization program,” Walther said. “I would argue, regardless of Gen. LaNeve coming into this position, the force was ready for clarification. They had done enough experimentation at the lowest echelons, and so some kind of deliberate framework from HQDA [headquarters of the Department of the Army] was needed and wanted.”
“We’re not leaving modernization behind, and there’s lots of avenues to continue to experiment throughout. But we need focus,” he added.
A former brigade innovation officer, who served as a captain, told Breaking Defense in a recent interview that he witnessed soldiers facing tech fatigue as they were only given new tech just as they were leaving for CTCs.
“They got pushed this equipment. They never had a chance to train on it. There was a big thing because they were TIC 1.0 brigade, and Gen. George was in attendance […] there was pressure to really get these guys to show off this new equipment, and it kind of became less of a value for the soldiers and much more of a distraction and a show and tell exercise,” they said.
The former captain, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, also said that sometimes brigade commanders would receive equipment that didn’t necessarily meet a mission requirement, creating confusion on why they were made to experiment with something that didn’t have an assigned purpose, or sometimes it simply wouldn’t work.
An industry executive who participated in CTCs shared similar concerns, noting that soldiers were sometimes given technology without knowing how to use it or what problem it was intended to solve.
“There’s a lot of solutions that are looking for problems,” the industry exec said. “That’s where the tech fatigue comes — there’s a lot of over-engineered solutions that don’t really solve a problem or optimize the reality of how the soldier fights”
The industry official highlighted another issue, when units are given tech that’s not yet ready for soldier use, whether that means it’s not yet ruggedized or it can’t connect to the Army’s command and control networks.
“Is it ready for me to include into a [CTC] rotation? Leaders go there to get certified to be leaders in combat, and so if it’s no kidding, something my guys or gals will take out into the field and put on the truck to take to the fight. Then that’s what I want,” they said.
A New 180 Day Mandate
Another major change under “How the Army Fights” is a requirement that soldiers receive experimentation tech that leaders want to test during CTCs at least 180 days before they leave for such exercises. Previously, there was no deadline for introducing new equipment before these large-scale combat training exercises, Walther said.
Lt. Gen. James Isenhower, commanding general of the Army Combined Arms Command, previewed such changes in September. He explained that the Army wants to be more “careful” with the experimentation requirements they put on the rotational force, or the BlueFOR, and giving them time to integrate before CTC should do the trick.
The BlueFOR will still test experimental tech, but a portion of what was dumped on them will now be sent to the opposition force, who “fights” the BlueFOR in CTCs. He said this is because the opposition force is generally stationed at training locations, so they have more time to become accustomed to experimental tech before they have to participate in CTCs.
Isenhower told reporters in a September call that the Army is making this change so the rotational force can focus on their own processes, standards and operating procedures to ensure they are “tactically proficient” and to avoid tech fatigue.
“We’ve had a couple of examples in the recent past where we’ve given new technology to units just as they were entering what we call ‘the box,’” he said. “The reality is, we owe them more time so they can integrate that equipment and focus on fighting the enemy as opposed to what oftentimes is a focus on simply trying to understand the equipment,” Isenhower said in September.
The former captain said the new 180 day mandate could be a promising solution to alleviate tech fatigue. But, they said, the rule shouldn’t focus so much on a distinct timeline, but instead the blueprint should be, “if you aren’t trained and certified on that technology during your culminating brigade exercise prior to CTCs, then you absolutely should not be able to incorporate that.”
Ultimately, LaNeve’s approach with “How the Army Fights” is intended to ensure that soldiers receive new tech with adequate preparation before they enter CTCs, such tech comes with a clearer purpose from top leaders and it has a defined place within the Army’s broader warfighting structure.
“This is about the Department of the Army saying, ‘This is how we’re going to fight. This is how we’re going to man train and equip you. This is your doctrine.’’ That theoretically will “alleviate a lot of the tech fatigue that the force is starting to feel,” Walther said.

articles.title: Colorado says cyberattack took down myColorado app, warns 150,000 had data stolen
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Cybercriminals likely stole data from 150,000 users of myColorado, which residents typically use for digital identification, document storage and accessing state government services.
articles.full_text:
Colorado says cyberattack took down myColorado app, warns 150,000 had data stolen
A critical app used by thousands of Colorado residents for state services was taken down by a cyberattack last week.
The Governor’s Office of Information Technology (OIT) said the incident was discovered on the evening of November 18 and involved hackers breaching the myColorado app — which Colorado residents use for digital identification, document storage and accessing state government services.
OIT shut down the app and began an investigation. The app is still unavailable as of Tuesday afternoon.
The state noted that the app has 2.1 million users and the cyberattack likely involved the theft of data tied to nearly 150,000 people. Investigators declined to provide more information about what data may have been stolen by the cybercriminals.
“We know how much Coloradans rely on these services, and we understand how this is frustrating and inconvenient. Protecting our users’ data is our first priority, and we will bring systems back online as quickly as we can once security is restored,” said Sarah Tuneberg, executive director of OIT.
Colorado urged residents to bring their physical IDs if they are traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday.
Those seeking to access state services can still do so through Colorado agency websites.
The state previously dealt with major cyberattacks on the Department of Higher Education and ransomware attacks on several smaller municipalities.
Several city and state governments are currently dealing with ransomware attacks and cyber incidents, including agencies in New York, Mississippi and California. On Friday, West Virginia’s legislature was knocked offline due to a cyberattack.
Queens Public Library in New York City confirmed it has nearly recovered from a ransomware attack two weeks ago that shut down services at its 66 branches. The library, which serves the borough’s more than 2 million residents, has been forced to operate without digital services.
The attack was claimed on Sunday by The Gentlemen ransomware gang — a cybercriminal group that claimed 398 attacks last quarter. The group far surpassed all other ransomware gangs with the amount of claimed victims, according to researchers at Halcyon.
In Mississippi, Lauderdale County’s more than 70,000 residents were also impacted by a cyberattack on the sheriff’s office on Monday.
The law enforcement agency said it was forced to take its systems offline after the cyberattack. Several services, including the inmate roster listing, are no longer available to the public.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: California privacy agency director Kemp to leave after two-year tenure
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The director of the trailblazing California Privacy Protection Agency announced his departure following implementation of a first-in-the-nation platform allowing consumers to easily opt out of data sharing.
articles.full_text:
California privacy agency director Kemp to leave after two-year tenure
The director of the trailblazing California Privacy Protection Agency (CalPrivacy) on Tuesday announced his departure after nearly two years leading the organization as it implemented a first-in-the-nation platform allowing consumers to easily opt out of data sharing.
Tom Kemp made the announcement in a LinkedIn post highlighting his work on the so-called Delete Request and Opt-Out Platform (DROP). The system is now used by more than 600,000 Californians who can block data sharing and foil data brokers with the push of a button.
The platform debuted in January, but penalties for companies violating consumers’ data privacy wishes only went into effect in August. Each DROP user has, on average, forced more than 200 deletions by data brokers, Kemp said.
He will begin a new position in January, but did not disclose any details about his new role.
“I am proud that CalPrivacy under my tenure has made great progress in making it significantly easier for Californians to exercise their privacy rights, and that our work represents a case study of how to deliver innovative government services that can make a tangible difference,” he said.
Under Kemp’s stewardship, CalPrivacy also led the push to pass two pieces of legislation expanding consumer privacy, lobbied against federal preemption of California’s tough privacy laws and oversaw the issuance of the largest fine in CalPrivacy’s history.
The agency also adopted the country’s most comprehensive regulations mandating how industry deploys cybersecurity audits, risk assessments and automated decisionmaking technology. The latter refers to software, including algorithms and AI, that processes personal data to make decisions about individuals relating to employment and other significant events.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Lawmakers warn ID verification companies to bolster security after September hack
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A bicameral, bipartisan letter from lawmakers said identity verification companies still have significant security work to do in the wake of a data breach at IDscan in September.
articles.full_text:
Lawmakers warn ID verification companies to bolster security after September hack
A bipartisan group of federal lawmakers on Monday sent a letter focused on security practices to several identity verification companies, citing a September breach that led to scans of more than 150 million people’s drivers’ licenses and other identification documents appearing for sale on the dark web.
The breach of IDScan led to the theft of customer data stored in the company’s cloud platform, spurring an FBI probe and identity theft and fraud concerns for the vast number of Canadian and U.S. victims.
The six lawmakers behind the letter pressured the identity verification firms to provide detailed answers about how they manage customers’ sensitive data and what they are doing to protect it against increasingly common and devastating hacks enabled by artificial intelligence.
They cited not only the risk of fraud and identity theft, but also pointed to the fact that foreign adversaries are increasingly able to “infer Americans’ behavior through commercial data linked to government credentials,” said the letter, signed by Sens. Brian Schatz (D-HI) and Marcia Blackburn (R-TN) with four others from the Senate and House.
“Given the difficulty of tracking these credentials and data sales, remedying this breach will pose substantial challenges even where no further crime is committed.”
Brian Krebs, the independent technology journalist who first reported the IDScan breach in September, said on social media Tuesday that in the past couple of months he has found more than two dozen identity verification companies that store scanned IDs, often by default.
Customers — the companies verifying users’ identities — often have to pay more to avoid the scans from continuing to be collected after verification, Krebs said.
Cybercriminals on the Russia-tied dark web marketplace Nexus began exfiltrating the data more than a year before officials discovered the purloined information online, Krebs reported.
In their letter, the lawmakers directed the identity verification companies to lessen risks by proactively hunting for system vulnerabilities, deploying zero-trust architecture and minimizing threats by limiting collection, sharing and storage of personally identifying information as much as possible.
“This breach’s scale warrants additional attention to the data-handling practices of companies like yours,” a letter to IDScan CEO Jimmy Roussel said, noting that in addition to the identification documents nearly 600,000 medical cards, employment authorizations and other sensitive data was exposed.
Many of the medical cards were for marijuana dispensaries, Krebs reported.
The peddled license scans included ultraviolet, infrared and other detailed images, intensifying worries about how criminals may use it.
A spokesperson for IDScan did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The lawmakers also emphasized that the personally identifiable information marketed by Nexus included scans belonging to high-ranking military and intelligence officials.
“The consequences of this theft may be widespread and persistent,” the letter to Roussel said.
“Given the difficulty of tracking these credentials and data sales, remedying this breach will pose substantial challenges even where no further crime is committed.”
“Your duty to safeguard data is critical in light of AI-driven cyberattack capabilities, which may be utilized by cybercriminals for zero-day exploits.”
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace says third-party breach leaked donation info
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Some donors to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace had their information leaked due to a cyberattack on a third-party vendor named Soapbox Engage.
articles.full_text:
Carnegie Endowment for International Peace says third-party breach leaked donation info
Some donors to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace had their information leaked due to a cyberattack on a third-party vendor named Soapbox Engage.
The organization sent emails to past donors on Friday warning of the data breach, writing that the incident occurred on October 28. The threat actors were removed from the vendor’s system on October 30, they said.
Carnegie Endowment for International Peace spokesperson Sharmeen Aly confirmed to Recorded Future News that the vendor was Soapbox Engage — an online fundraising and engagement software platform for nonprofits.
Carnegie uses Soapbox Engage for online donations. The hackers stole names, email addresses, phone numbers and giving history.
“Due to an integration with Carnegie's database, the unauthorized users were able to temporarily gain access to contact information maintained by Carnegie,” Aly said. “Based on our investigation, a small percentage of our database was affected. No full credit card numbers were exposed.”
Aly added that the organization notified everyone in their database about the breach due to European data privacy laws. Carnegie hired a cybersecurity firm to confirm the hackers were removed from the system.
Aly did not say how many people were impacted by the incident. Founded in 1910, the think tank currently employs more than 200 experts. The institute supports research efforts, diplomacy and more.
In its last financial statement, the non-profit declared more than $522 million in assets and an operating revenue of about $51 million.
Soapbox Engage did not respond to requests for comment but the incident coincides with the disclosure of data breaches and cyberattacks by multiple digital donation platforms.
Fundraising software company DonorPerfect said it was impacted by a security incident last week, and on Friday GoFundMe said it identified a cybersecurity incident where hackers breached their systems in two separate attacks in October and November. GoFundMe reported the cyberattack to law enforcement.
“We have reviewed the data involved, and determined it included limited personal information such as names, postal addresses, phone numbers and, for some, dates of birth or other information provided voluntarily in registration forms,” the company said.
No card numbers or bank details were exposed and GoFundMe said they “addressed the known methods of unauthorized access, disabled unauthorized accounts, and are actively monitoring for further suspicious activity.”
In its statement, GoFundMe said the recent attacks on other fundraising platforms were evidence that organizations had to do a better job of protecting donor information.
“To help prevent something like this from happening again, we are identifying opportunities to further strengthen the safeguards protecting our platform and are using those findings to guide additional security improvements designed to help prevent similar incidents,” the company said.
The Nonprofit Times news outlet reported that the recent attacks on the fundraising platforms appeared to be coordinated and at least one incident involved the theft of funds.

articles.title: CISA warns of exploited N-able bug as company restores email platform
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The U.S. cyber agency is giving government departments until Thanksgiving to patch a vulnerability impacting a critical email security platform that blocks spam, malware and other threats.
articles.full_text:
CISA warns of exploited N-able bug as company restores email platform
The federal cybersecurity agency is giving U.S. government departments until Thanksgiving to patch a vulnerability impacting a critical email security platform that blocks spam, malware and other threats.
All federal agencies were urged to patch CVE-2026-134624 – a bug affecting N-able’s Mail Assure platform. The vulnerability carries a 9.3 severity score and was added to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) exploited vulnerabilities platform on Monday evening.
N-able has dealt with a week of outages tied to the vulnerability after hackers breached one of the company’s servers through the bug, causing damage to Mail Assure and SpamExperts services.
In a statement to Recorded Future News, N-able said it remediated the bug over the weekend and restored access to internal dashboards for customers.
Inbound and outbound email flow and spam filtering continued to operate throughout the incident, they added.
“Since completing these remediation actions, we have continued scanning and monitoring the Mail Assure environments and have found no evidence of exploitation beyond the single N-able-hosted server identified in our initial investigation,” a spokesperson said, adding that they hired incident responders to validate their findings.
The company pledged to publish a root cause analysis within the next two weeks.
N-able said the breach and service issues are not connected to more than 30 vulnerabilities impacting its N-central platform that were publicicized two weeks ago by a security researcher.
N-central is a popular remote management tool that thousands of IT teams use to monitor and run networks remotely. N-able took all hosted N-central environments offline and ordered customers to turn off their servers.
A bug in the company’s N-central platform was involved in a supply-chain attack by ransomware actors in August.
N-able was previously a business unit within software company SolarWinds before it was spun off as a separate cloud-based software solutions company offering tools to managed service providers.

articles.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
articles.snippet: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use "advanced cryptographic tools" to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
articles.full_text:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”
But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].
The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.
The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.
The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.
Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.
A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.
But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.
“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”
Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.
In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.
“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”
The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.
“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”
Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.
“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”
The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.
Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
